teaser: A hand pressing into a body. Both are stone, and only one of them looks like it.
review_notes:
In this photo (taken from the statue's left side) the hand visible pressing into Proserpina's body is the one at her waist/flank; the more famous grip on her thigh is on the other side. Spot texts describe only what this angle shows.
Cerberus is seen from behind in this photo: only its hindquarters and what appears to be its tail are visible between Pluto's legs; please check the 'Cerberus' and 'tail' spots against the image.
The two-pronged fork on the base is read as Pluto's bident: check.
Marble tears on Proserpina's cheek exist on the sculpture but cannot be seen at this resolution; mentioned in text only.
Dates: carved 1621 to 1622 when Bernini was 23; given by Scipione Borghese to Cardinal Ludovico Ludovisi in 1622; bought by the Italian state and returned to the Galleria Borghese in 1908: to verify.
Height about 2.55 m.
Pietro Bernini as the trainer of his son, and the boy carving from childhood: standard account.
The title uses 'rape' in the old sense of the Latin raptus (seizure, abduction); the museum's Italian title is Ratto di Proserpina.

lesson.text: How hard would you have to squeeze a rock before your fingers left a dent in it? The question sounds silly. Hold on to it anyway, because a sculptor in Rome answered it in 1622, and visitors have been leaning in to check his answer ever since.

The group shows two figures a little larger than life, about 2.55 meters (8 feet 4 inches) with the base. A bearded, crowned man strides forward carrying a young woman who fights to get free. All of it, bodies, hair, cloth and ground, is one piece of white marble from Carrara, in Tuscany.
Somewhere on this statue, marble behaves like soft flesh under pressure. Tap the place.

spots.title: The grip
spots.text: His fingers sink into her side, and the stone swells between them like skin. Marble cannot give way, of course. Bernini carved the dent, the bulge and the shadow.

lesson.text: That is the answer to the opening question: you cannot dent stone, but you can carve the dent. Gian Lorenzo Bernini was twenty-three. He polished her skin to a soft glow and gave the man's hand hard knuckles and tendons, so the two surfaces look like different materials.

Bernini grew up with a chisel in his hand. His father Pietro was a sculptor who brought the family to Rome to work for the pope, and the boy was carving marble heads before he was a teenager. By his early twenties he had a cardinal for a patron and a workshop of his own.

The man is Pluto, god of the underworld, the kingdom of the dead. The woman is Proserpina, daughter of Ceres, goddess of the harvest. In the myth he bursts out of the earth while she is picking flowers and carries her below to be his queen.

About the title: “rape” here keeps the old meaning of the Latin word raptus, a seizing or carrying off. In Italian the work is called the Ratto, the abduction. Bernini does not soften it. He builds the whole group out of two forces that cannot both win.

lines.label: His drive
lines.text: From the back foot through the thigh and chest to the head, Pluto's body is one slanted beam, shoving forward and up.

lines.label: Her push
lines.text: Her arm is locked straight against his head, and her own head pulls as far the other way as it can. This line leaves his at a sharp angle: the two bodies are tearing apart.

lines.label: No ground
lines.text: Her legs hang and kick in the air, with nothing under them. Her only point of support is the body she is trying to escape.

lesson.text: A group pulling in two directions has a practical problem: it has to stand. Nearly all the weight lands on Pluto's two legs. Bernini adds a third support behind them and disguises it as a character from the story.
Bernini treats marble as if it were several materials: soft skin, wiry hair, limp cloth, rough earth. The contrast between those textures is what makes the scene feel real.

The patron, Cardinal Scipione Borghese, hardly had time to enjoy it. In 1622, soon after it was finished, he gave the statue to the nephew of the newly elected pope, a useful gesture in Roman politics. It only came back to the Borghese villa in 1908.

The myth does not end in the dark. Ceres, searching for her daughter, lets the crops die. A deal is struck: Proserpina, who has eaten a few pomegranate seeds below, will spend part of each year with Pluto and the rest above ground. Her return is spring. For the ancients, this was why seasons exist.

On the real statue, marble tears run down her cheek. They are too small to see in this photograph, taken from the side. Plenty of other details are within reach, including that disguised support and a weapon Pluto has dropped.

spots.title: Her hand on his brow
spots.text: She shoves against his forehead, right under the spikes of his crown, forcing his head to tilt. He keeps going.

spots.title: The beard
spots.text: Deep, drilled curls that trap shadow. Next to the smooth skin of her arm, the hair looks coarse and almost alive.

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Turned away as far as her neck allows, hair streaming back. From the front of the statue you would see her open mouth and her tears.

spots.title: The raised arm
spots.text: A long, thin limb of marble thrown into empty space. Each finger is carved free. It is the most fragile part of the group and the highest.

spots.title: Kicking feet
spots.text: Her toes spread and curl with effort. Feet carved off the ground were a show of confidence: there is nothing beneath them but air.

spots.title: Cerberus
spots.text: The mass behind Pluto's legs is Cerberus, the three-headed dog that guards the underworld. From this side you see its hindquarters. It is also the hidden support that keeps the group standing.

spots.title: The dropped fork
spots.text: A two-pronged fork lies flat on the ground under his stride. It is Pluto's scepter, let go because he needs both hands.

spots.title: The braced leg
spots.text: Knee bent, calf tight, heel dug in. This leg takes the load of two bodies, and Bernini shows every muscle doing its job.

quiz.question: How old was Bernini when he finished this group?
quiz.explanation: He carved it in 1621 and 1622, at twenty-three.

quiz.question: What does “rape” mean in the traditional title?
options: A seizing or carrying off, from the Latin raptus
quiz.explanation: The title keeps the old sense of abduction, as in the Italian Ratto.

quiz.question: What hides the extra support behind Pluto's legs?
quiz.explanation: The three-headed guard dog of the underworld doubles as a structural prop.

quiz.question: In the myth, what does Proserpina's yearly return explain?
quiz.explanation: Her time below is winter and her return is spring.

quiz.question: What did Cardinal Borghese do with the statue in 1622?
options: He sold it to the king of France
He gave it to the new pope's nephew
He had it buried in his garden
quiz.explanation: He gave it away as a political gift, and it returned to the villa only in 1908.

facts.text: Bernini used a softer stone for Proserpina's body than for Pluto's hand.
facts.explanation: The whole group is one piece of Carrara marble; the softness is carved illusion.

facts.text: Pluto's fork lies on the ground because he needs both hands.
facts.explanation: The two-pronged scepter has been dropped on the base under his stride.

facts.text: Proserpina's feet rest firmly on a rock.
facts.explanation: Her legs kick in the air with nothing beneath them.
